To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
individual differences in age-related cognitive decline are associated with individual differences in brain structure and functional integrity.

the neural substrates of cognitive function are differentially affected by aging, that individual differences in age-related changes in these substrates are associated with individual differences in the magnitude of cognitive decline, and that these individual differences in the neural correlates of cognitive function are not necessarily related to the degree of cognitive impairment.
Individuals with normal aging who are cognitively intact show little or no decline in the volume of brain regions associated with memory function.
In summary, our research is concerned with
identifying the neurobiological mechanisms underlying individual differences in age-related changes in cognitive function.
identifying individual differences in cognitive function in normal aging, and the neural basis of these differences.
identifying the neurobiological basis of cognitive dysfunction in aging and with determining how these changes relate to individual differences in cognitive performance.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
aging is not necessarily accompanied by cognitive decline, but it is by a reduction in the cognitive reserve capacity of the brain.
the cognitive and neuroanatomical effects of aging are not uniform across all individuals, and that the degree to which aging leads to cognitive decline is dependent on the individual.
there is an age-related decline in the efficiency of cognitive processing.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
individual differences in the cognitive consequences of normal aging can be accounted for by differences in brain structure and/or function.
the cognitive changes that are associated with aging are not uniform across individuals and that the underlying neural changes are also not uniform across subjects.

individual differences in cognitive function in normal aging are related to individual differences in the structure of the medial temporal lobe and in the functional integrity of the medial temporal-lobe memory circuit.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the cognitive and neural consequences of normal aging are highly individual.
individual differences in age-related changes in cognitive and brain function are substantial.

the neural correlates of age-related cognitive decline are heterogeneous, and that the neural mechanisms that are associated with normal aging are not necessarily those that are associated with cognitive decline.
